title: Device characterization of Si$/$SiGe double quantum dots using exchange oscillations in Earth's magnetic field
authors: Holly G. Stemp, Harry Hanlim Kang, Chih Hwan Yang, Gabriel D. Cutter, Frederike Brockmeyer, Patrick J. Strohbeen, Max Hays, Jeffrey A. Grover, William D. Oliver
abstract: Exchange-based semiconductor qubits encompass a broad family of encodings constructed from singlet- and triplet-like spin states, several of which are compatible with operation at zero applied magnetic field. Their reliable operation requires characterization of environmental noise, residual idle interactions, and exchange-dependent decay, but this characterization often relies on multi-axis control calibration or deliberately engineered magnetic-field gradients. A simpler zero-applied-field diagnostic is particularly valuable for hybrid semiconductor-superconductor systems, in which magnetic fields can degrade superconducting components. Here, we use the intrinsic magnetic-field gradient produced by residual nuclear spins in isotopically enriched Si/SiGe to implement exchange oscillations between two quantum dots as a characterization tool without a micromagnet, dynamic nuclear polarization, or prior multi-axis calibration. Using Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill exchange sequences, we extend the singlet coherence from $T_2^*=1.17\pm0.02~μ$s to $T_2^{\mathrm{CPMG}}=74.8\pm1.8~μ$s with $N=70$ refocusing pulses. The oscillation phase resolves residual exchange in the tens-of-kilohertz regime and enables it to be mapped across the $(1,1)$ charge cell. These results establish intrinsic-gradient exchange oscillations as a simple, more relevant zero-field diagnostic for exchange-only and related semiconductor qubit encodings that is amenable to rapid, high-throughput device characterization.
summary: This paper presents a novel, field-free method to characterize spin qubits in Si/SiGe double quantum dots by exploiting the intrinsic magnetic field gradient from nuclear spins. By implementing CPMG exchange sequences, the researchers significantly extend coherence times and accurately map the residual exchange coupling. This establishes a simple, highly relevant diagnostic technique for next-generation solid-state quantum computing devices.
main_problem: The primary goal was to develop a simple, zero-applied-field diagnostic method to characterize exchange-coupled spin pairs in semiconductor qubits, especially for hybrid systems sensitive to external magnetic fields.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that intrinsic magnetic-field gradients from residual nuclear spins can be used to implement exchange oscillations, extending coherence times significantly and providing a simple, high-throughput characterization tool.
method: The characterization relies on applying Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) exchange sequences to measure the decay and oscillation phase of the singlet state coherence.
model_or_system: The system is based on Si/SiGe double quantum dots (DQD) used as semiconductor qubits. The physics is modeled using an effective Hamiltonian restricted to the $\{|Sangle, |T_0angle\}$ subspace, incorporating the intrinsic gradient ($\Delta B_z$) and exchange coupling ($J$).
key_observables: Singlet coherence time ($T_{CPMG}^2$), residual exchange coupling ($J_{res}$), and the frequency/Q-factor of exchange oscillations.
important_parameters: Coherence times up to $75 \mu$s; residual exchange coupling resolved in the tens-of-kilohertz regime; exchange tunability of $\sim 5.2 	ext{ dec/V}$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the intrinsic gradient from residual nuclear spins provides a sufficient, quasi-static quantization axis, allowing the use of CPMG sequences without external magnets.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the pulse sequence logic for generating exchange oscillations, and quantitative results showing the extension of coherence time via CPMG and the extraction of $J_{res}$ via joint fitting of multiple pulse sequences.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for zero-field diagnostics, then detailing the use of CPMG sequences to measure coherence, followed by advanced fitting techniques to extract residual exchange coupling ($J_{res}$), and concluding with the characterization of exchange tunability.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust, practical diagnostic tool for solid-state qubits, directly addressing the challenge of operating in environments (like superconducting circuits) where external magnetic fields are detrimental, which is highly relevant to quantum computing hardware development.
